info.name: Great Amphitheatre
info.text: Three storeys of arches, thirteen rings of stone seats and room for sixteen hundred on its own paved square. It has a gate for the living and a gate for the dead, and only one of them is ever busy both ways.

info.name: Arena Exit
info.text: The way out, with a bucket for the faint of stomach. It is emptied after every fight, and it is never empty.

info.name: Arena Entrance
info.text: The ticket hut, skull on the roof. Seats are numbered, limbs are not.

info.name: Arena
info.text: A round sand pit with a stone ring and three rows of planks. Men walk in through the gate; how many walk out is up to the gods and the crowd.

info.name: Sand Pit
info.text: The first arena: a ring of planks around a pit of sand on its own square plot, a lanista's box and two sails for the nobility. Three to a seat, one way in, two ways out.

info.name: Sand Pit
info.text: The first arena, now with neighbours: a ring of planks in a rectangle of sheds, patched tents and puddles. Nobody knows who lives in them, and nobody has ever come out to complain about the noise.

info.name: Armoury
info.text: Every blade counted, every lock bronze. The count is always one short.

info.name: Bacchant Vine
info.text: A wild tangle of vines with near-black berries and a torn ivy wreath. Eat one and dance, eat three and dance forever.

info.name: Bacchant Vine (amphora)
info.text: An empty amphora lies in the weeds. The worshippers drank the wine and then the evidence.

info.name: Bacchant Vine (altar)
info.text: A small stone altar, stained purple, with a bronze cup. The god of excess accepts any offering, as long as it is too much.

info.name: Barracks
info.text: Bunks for twenty, smell for forty. The tally by the door is not for days served.

info.name: Acacia
info.text: A flat-topped acacia, the only shade for a day in any direction. Lions, vultures and travellers all agree on that, and they rarely agree on anything else.

info.name: Acacia, Helmet Hook
info.text: Someone hung a bronze helmet on this acacia and never came back for it. Shade for one, ventilation included.

info.name: Acacia, Picnic Leftovers
info.text: An acacia with a few bleached bones at its foot. Lunch was had here once, just not by the traveller.

info.name: Acacia, Dry Season
info.text: A parched acacia with rust-brown leaves, a frayed rope stub and three red rags. The local tourist board calls it a landmark.

info.name: Apple Tree
info.text: Red apples, free for the taking. The worms were here first and they are not sharing.

info.name: Apple Tree, Windfall
info.text: Ripe apples above, rotting apples below. The tree knows the arena crowd will throw either.

info.name: Apple Tree, Helmet Basket
info.text: A dented helmet makes a fine fruit basket. The previous owner no longer needs it to keep anything in.

info.name: Apple Tree, Tally Board
info.text: An old, half-bare apple tree with a board nailed to it, tallying something. Nobody admits what, and the bones nearby are not talking.

info.name: Baobab
info.text: A baobab with a trunk like a wine jar. Hollow inside, which the locals use for storing water, grain and the occasional tax collector.

info.name: Baobab, Chained
info.text: A baobab wrapped in iron chain with a padlock. Either the tree is valuable or something inside it is not allowed out.

info.name: Baobab, Scoreboard
info.text: Rows of tally marks carved into the bark and old bones at the roots. The baobab keeps score better than the referee.

info.name: Baobab, Dry Season
info.text: A leafless baobab with a shut plank door and a frayed rope stub. The door is locked from the outside, which says a lot.

info.name: Birch
info.text: A pale birch. Its rods are flexible, cheap and well remembered by every recruit.

info.name: Birch, Counted
info.text: A birch with fresh tally marks among its natural black ones. Some recruit is counting the days, or the rods.

info.name: Birch, Target Practice
info.text: A birch with an arrow stuck in its trunk. It was not the target; the target ran.

info.name: Birch, Snapped
info.text: A birch with a broken crown and yellowing leaves. It lost a fight with the wind and, judging by the bone, so did someone else.

info.name: Beech
info.text: A broad beech with a smooth grey trunk. Burns long and hot, which the smith appreciates more than the beech does.

info.name: Beech, Crossed Heart
info.text: A carved heart, crossed out in red. Love is short, beech bark is patient.

info.name: Beech, Stuck Sword
info.text: A sword driven into the trunk, a little blood below. Whoever pulls it out becomes king, or at least the next to bleed.

info.name: Beech, Autumn Copper
info.text: A copper-leaved beech in autumn, with tally marks and a red stain at its foot. The leaves are not the only thing that fell here.

info.name: Date Palm
info.text: A tall palm heavy with dates. Sweet enough for a senator, and the climb is steep enough to cull the greedy.

info.name: Date Palm, Shield Nail
info.text: A date palm with a round bronze shield nailed to it. Excellent cover, as long as the enemy stands exactly there.

info.name: Date Palm, Withered Skirt
info.text: A leaning date palm hung with dead brown fronds. Fashionable among palms, flammable among everyone.

info.name: Date Palm, Climbing Notches
info.text: Notches cut for climbing, red dates at the top and a stain at the bottom. The last notch was one too many.

info.name: Old Oak
info.text: An oak older than the empire and twice as honest. Its roots have drunk from more battlefields than any legionary. Excellent shade, terrible witness.

info.name: Old Oak, Trophy Branch
info.text: A bronze helmet on one branch, a sword in the trunk. The oak collects armour the way other trees collect moss.

info.name: Old Oak, Hollow
info.text: A hollow oak with bones tucked inside. Hide-and-seek champion, posthumously.

info.name: Old Oak, Lightning Struck
info.text: Half dead after a lightning strike, charred down the middle, a frayed rope still tied to a bare limb. The gods aimed at the rope.

info.name: Tree Fern
info.text: A fern grown tall enough to call itself a tree. It was old when the gods were young and has not been impressed since.

info.name: Tree Fern, Broken Spear
info.text: A tree fern with a broken spear shaft caught in its fronds. The fern survived the dinosaurs; this spear did not survive the fern.

info.name: Tree Fern, Wilting
info.text: A tree fern going brown at the edges. Too much sun, too little rain, and far too much arena runoff.

info.name: Tree Fern, Lost Blade
info.text: A short gladius rusting among the roots, with a little blood on the soil. Someone dropped it, and then everything else.

info.name: Coconut Palm
info.text: A leaning palm with a crown of coconuts. Every year it drops one on somebody, and every year the priests call it a sign.

info.name: Coconut Palm B
info.text: A palm leaning a little less than its neighbours. It still drops coconuts with the same aim.

info.name: Coconut Palm C (helmet)
info.text: A fallen coconut lies next to a dented bronze helmet. The helmet lost.

info.name: Coconut Palm D (tally)
info.text: A palm with dry brown fronds and a tally scratched into the trunk. Nobody knows what is being counted, only that it keeps rising.

info.name: Liana Tree
info.text: A jungle tree hung with lianas. Good for swinging, better for hanging, and nobody here ever bothers to tell the two apart.

info.name: Liana Tree B (chain)
info.text: A jungle giant with a rusty chain and an open shackle hanging from a branch. Whoever wore it climbed better than the guards.

info.name: Liana Tree C (strangler)
info.text: A strangler fig slowly squeezing its host to death. The arena masters study it for business ideas.

info.name: Liana Tree D (spear)
info.text: A broken spear juts from the trunk among red blossoms. The beast hunt missed; the tree took the blow.

info.name: Mangrove
info.text: A mangrove standing on its roots in the brine. The crabs live underneath, the mosquitoes above, and lost sandals in between.

info.name: Mangrove B
info.text: A mangrove on extra stilts over a smaller mud pool. It stands in the water so nothing can sneak up on it.

info.name: Mangrove C (net)
info.text: A torn fishing net snagged in the roots and a dented bronze helmet in the mud. The fishing was poor, the fight was worse.

info.name: Mangrove D (oar)
info.text: An oar stuck upright in the mud between the roots. The boat is gone, and so is the rower.

info.name: Olive Tree
info.text: A gnarled olive tree, older than the oldest grudge in town. Oil for the lamps, oil for the wounds, oil for the bribes.

info.name: Olive Tree B (hollow)
info.text: An old olive with a hollow trunk. Smugglers, lovers and debtors have all hidden in it, rarely at the same time.

info.name: Olive Tree C (curses)
info.text: Little lead curse tablets are nailed to this olive. Each one asks the gods to break a rival's legs before the games.

info.name: Olive Tree D (half dead)
info.text: Half of this olive died, a frayed rope still tied to a bare branch. Nobody in the village admits to owning the rope.

info.name: Poplar
info.text: A tall, thin poplar. Soft wood, fast growth and no character at all, rather like a senator.

info.name: Poplar B
info.text: A thinner poplar, leaves rattling in every breeze. The crowd sounds just like it when a gladiator falls.

info.name: Poplar C (dead top)
info.text: A poplar whose top died standing. Bare twigs point at the sky like a referee who has seen enough.

info.name: Poplar D (notice)
info.text: A poplar with a wanted notice nailed to it and an arrow through the notice. Someone found the man first.

info.name: Fir
info.text: A dark fir, straight as a spear. Makes good beams, good masts and, if business is slow, good coffins.

info.name: Fir B
info.text: A younger fir with a few dead brown branches. It is learning early what the arena teaches everyone.

info.name: Fir C (axe)
info.text: A fir with a snapped crown and an axe still stuck in the trunk. The woodcutter left in a hurry and never came back for it.

info.name: Fir D (red rag)
info.text: A fir stripped of its lower branches, a red rag tied to a stub. Someone marked a grave here, or a debt.

info.name: Cypress
info.text: A slim dark cypress, the traditional tree of graveyards. It grows near the arena for the same reason.

info.name: Cypress B (bent)
info.text: A cypress with its tip bent by the wind. Even the graveyard trees bow to the emperor's weather.

info.name: Cypress C (split)
info.text: Lightning split this cypress into two spires. The priests charged for both omens.

info.name: Cypress D (grave)
info.text: A cypress guarding a small headstone with a wilted wreath. The name has worn off; the debt has not.

info.name: Beastrium
info.text: Three cages, all empty for now. The straw remembers what lived here, and so do the bones.

info.name: Straw Bed
info.text: A wooden frame, old straw and one blanket. The fleas were here first and they pay no rent either.

info.name: Shingled Roof Slope, Right
info.text: Split wooden shingles, grey with age and green with moss. Light, cheap and as loyal as a hired guard.

info.name: Shingle Right A
info.text: Moss creeps along the shingle edges. In ten years it will own the house; it already pays more tax.

info.name: Shingle Right B
info.text: Patched with old shingles from a burnt barn. Nobody asked the barn.

info.name: Shingle Right C
info.text: A field stone weighs the shingles down against the storms. Sometimes against a lid.

info.name: Shingle Front E
info.text: A carpet of moss on the shingles. It holds the roof together better than the nails do.

info.name: Shingle Front F
info.text: An old axe sits in the roof since the inheritance was settled. Nobody dared to pull it out.

info.name: Shingle Front Ridge
info.text: A ridge board over the top shingles, nailed twice and prayed over once.

info.name: Log Window
info.text: A small window with heavy shutters. Small, because glass is dear and neighbours are curious.

info.name: Log Window A
info.text: One shutter hangs crooked on a single hinge. It bangs all night, which helps nobody sleep.

info.name: Log Window B
info.text: Boarded shut with a cross plank. Either the family left, or the family is hiding.

info.name: Log Window D
info.text: An arrow in the shutter and a dark streak below. The hunting season had a slow start.

info.name: Log Gable
info.text: The gable is stacked from shorter logs. Every winter it creaks a little more like an old man.

info.name: Log Gable A
info.text: A smoke hole under the roof. The smoke rarely finds it.

info.name: Log Gable Peak (down)
info.text: Top of a log gable, the other way round. The axe was no sharper.

info.name: Log Gable Peak (up)
info.text: Top of a log gable, cut to the slope of the roof with a dull axe.

info.name: Log Gable B
info.text: Carved notches against bad luck. Bad luck cannot read.

info.name: Log Gable C
info.text: A skull nailed under the roof. Officially to scare off spirits, unofficially a former tax collector.

info.name: Log Door
info.text: Planks, iron bands and a row of chalk marks. Each mark is a debt; each debt has a name.

info.name: Log Door A
info.text: An axe is stuck in the door frame. It was a discussion about firewood. The firewood won.

info.name: Log Wall
info.text: Round logs on a fieldstone footing, moss in the gaps. Keeps out wolves, debt collectors and most of the winter.

info.name: Log Wall A
info.text: One log was replaced. The old one went into the stove during the long winter, together with the chair.

info.name: Log Wall B
info.text: Moss grows in the chinks and a log has split. The owner calls it ventilation.

info.name: Log Wall D
info.text: A rusty trap hangs by the door, still stained. Nobody says what it caught last.

info.name: Log Upper Wall
info.text: Upper storey of stacked logs. Warm, solid and very easy to set on fire.

info.name: Log Upper Wall A
info.text: A coil of rope and a hatchet on a peg. Tools for trees, mostly.

info.name: Slate Floor
info.text: Cold slate, swept now and then. Spilled blood dries slowly up here.

info.name: Shingle Front A
info.text: Oak shingles under a fur of moss. The moss is the best-kept thing in town.

info.name: Shingle Front B
info.text: A patch of fresh shingles on old ones. Paid with the neighbour's fence.

info.name: Shingle Front C
info.text: Moss and shingles, roughly half and half. The moss is winning.

info.name: Shingle Front D
info.text: A hole where a shingle used to be. Something up there keeps borrowing them.

info.name: Shingle Front E
info.text: Stripped to the laths. The shingles went into somebody's stove last winter.

info.name: Shingle Front F
info.text: Blood runs down the shingles. The roofer fell, the roof held. Priorities.

info.name: Half-Timbered Window
info.text: A small window with a straw mat. Glass is for temples and fools.

info.name: Half-Timbered Window A
info.text: Boarded up from inside, the days scratched below. Somebody stopped counting.

info.name: Half-Timbered Window B
info.text: Same mat, newer braces. The carpenter was paid in turnips and built accordingly.

info.name: Half-Timbered Window D
info.text: The shutter hangs by one hinge and the scratches below go the wrong way. Nobody asks.

info.name: Half-Timbered Gable
info.text: Dark oak boards under the shingles. The owls hold the lease.

info.name: Half-Timbered Gable A
info.text: Oak rails and cracked whitewash under the roof. Cheaper to patch than to admit the house is old.

info.name: Half-Timbered Gable Peak (down)
info.text: The other half of the oak gable. It sags towards the neighbour out of spite.

info.name: Half-Timbered Gable Peak (up)
info.text: The pointed end of an oak gable. Woodpeckers keep trying it.

info.name: Half-Timbered Gable B
info.text: Oak rails and cracked whitewash under the roof. Cheaper to patch than to admit the house is old.

info.name: Half-Timbered Gable C
info.text: Oak rails and cracked whitewash under the roof. Cheaper to patch than to admit the house is old.

info.name: Half-Timbered Door
info.text: A heavy oak door with iron straps. Built to keep out wolves, tax men and the in-laws, in that order.

info.name: Half-Timbered Wall
info.text: Oak beams and whitewash over wattle. The beams are the only honest part of the house.

info.name: Half-Timbered Wall A
info.text: The plaster came off and the wattle shows. Nobody fixes it; it is the only window that never needs cleaning.

info.name: Half-Timbered Wall B
info.text: A crack runs from beam to beam. Below it someone counts the days in scratches. Or the debts.

info.name: Half-Timbered Wall D
info.text: Two chains on two nails, one of them still sticky. The landlord calls it a reminder.

info.name: Half-Timbered Upper Wall
info.text: An upper floor of oak crosses and whitewash. Leans over the lane so the neighbours can share the rain.

info.name: Half-Timbered Upper Wall A
info.text: A hook and a coil of rope, high up where the bailiff can see it. Subtle, as forest towns go.

info.name: Ploughed Field
info.text: Furrows of dark earth with green shoots. Somebody sweated here so somebody else can eat in the stands.

info.name: Quay Flagstones
info.text: Worn harbour flags, sand in every joint. Scrubbed twice a year, whether it needs it or not.

info.name: Quay Flagstones A
info.text: Shells, pebbles and a blob of tar. The sea leaves gifts; nobody asked for them.

info.name: Quay Flagstones B
info.text: A mismatched sandstone slab, borrowed from a grave nobody visits anymore.

info.name: Quay Flagstones C
info.text: A puddle that never dries. Locals call it the harbour master's bath.

info.name: Quay Flagstones D
info.text: A coil of rope and a rusty hook. Ask no questions about the last thing it held.

info.name: Quay Flagstones E
info.text: A bloodstain and a neat set of fishbones. The fishmonger and his customer disagreed on the price.

info.name: Quay Flagstones F
info.text: A broken slab with weed growing through. The town council has been meaning to fix it for forty years.

info.name: Slate Right
info.text: Blue-grey slates from the cliffs, quarried by men who are now at the bottom of them.

info.name: Slate Right A
info.text: Yellow lichen on wet slates. It grows faster than the fishermen's savings.

info.name: Slate Right B
info.text: Slates of three different quarries. The roofer calls it a pattern, the owner calls it robbery.

info.name: Slate Right C
info.text: Old slates, new slates, borrowed slates. Nobody asks where the borrowed ones came from.

info.name: Slate Right D
info.text: A hole in the slates with a broken oar stuck through it. The roofer drowned before he finished.

info.name: Slate Right E
info.text: Gull droppings, layered like a chronicle. Each storm washes a chapter away.

info.name: Slate Right F
info.text: A hole patched with a tarred plank from a wrecked boat. The boat had no further use for it.

info.name: Fishhouse Window
info.text: A small window with sea-blue shutters, paint flaking in the salt wind. Glass is for rich people.

info.name: Fishhouse Window A
info.text: Boarded up crosswise since the last storm. Or since the last visit from the harbour master.

info.name: Fishhouse Window B
info.text: A net slung under the sill and gull droppings down the boards. The gulls pay no rent either.

info.name: Fishhouse Window C
info.text: Cork floats strung under the sill, crusted with salt. A window with a view of other people's luck.

info.name: Fishhouse Window D
info.text: One shutter gone to the storm, a noose of net rope by the frame. Nobody in the house admits to tying it.

info.name: Fishhouse Window E
info.text: Nailed shut with two planks. The tenant left by sea, owing rent.

info.name: Fishhouse Window F
info.text: Boarded up and marked with a red cross. Fever, debt or both; nobody knocks to ask.

info.name: Fishhouse Gable
info.text: Gable boards nailed over the attic where the nets and the drowned man's savings are kept.

info.name: Fishhouse Gable A
info.text: Gable boards spattered by gulls. A badge of honour on this coast.

info.name: Fishhouse Gable Peak (down)
info.text: The falling verge, slate on tarred boards. Gulls sit here and judge the passers-by.

info.name: Fishhouse Gable Peak (down) A
info.text: Slates crusted white by gulls, edges ragged. The gulls own the roof; the family rents.

info.name: Fishhouse Gable Peak (down) B
info.text: Mossy slates, one slipped, one missing. Rain gets in, so do the rumours.

info.name: Fishhouse Gable Peak (down) C
info.text: A gap where a slate blew away. It was last seen at sea, like the owner.

info.name: Fishhouse Gable Peak (down) F
info.text: Lichen on uneven slates and a scrap of tarred rope. Held together by habit.

info.name: Fishhouse Gable Peak (up)
info.text: The rising verge, finished with a row of slates. The wind still finds its way in.

info.name: Fishhouse Gable Peak (up) A
info.text: Gull-whitened slates with ragged ends. The roof sings in the wind, badly.

info.name: Fishhouse Gable Peak (up) B
info.text: Moss on the rising verge, a slate askew. Fixed with the same nail three times.

info.name: Fishhouse Gable Peak (up) F
info.text: Lichen and a frayed rope end on the verge. The rope used to hold a sign. Then a man.

info.name: Fishhouse Gable B
info.text: Moss in the cracks of the gable boards. It is the only thing growing in this house.

info.name: Fishhouse Gable C
info.text: A board missing from the gable. The draught keeps the attic smelling of fish, not of the dead.

info.name: Fishhouse Gable F
info.text: Frayed rope ends caught on the gable nails. Nobody remembers what they held up.

info.name: Fishhouse Door
info.text: A plank door in a stone frame, swollen shut every spring. Knock twice, then shout over the gulls.

info.name: Fishhouse Door A
info.text: A coil of rope on a nail and an oar by the door. Ready to row out, or to beat the debt collector.

info.name: Fishhouse Door B
info.text: A rusty knocker and a tar bucket by the step. Mind the bucket, it bites.

info.name: Fishhouse Door C
info.text: Chalk tallies beside the frame and an oar against the wall. Each mark is a debt or a funeral.

info.name: Fishhouse Door D
info.text: A red handprint on the planks. Somebody wanted in very badly, once.

info.name: Fishhouse Door E
info.text: A heap of net and a basket blocking the step. Visitors are welcome to climb.

info.name: Fishhouse Wall
info.text: Tarred weatherboards on a fieldstone footing. Smells of fish, salt and whatever the tide left in the cellar.

info.name: Fishhouse Wall A
info.text: A torn net hung out to dry, corks and all. It has been drying since the owner went out and did not come back.

info.name: Fishhouse Wall B
info.text: A tar patch, a crust of salt and a spare oar. Every storm takes a board, every winter a fisherman.

info.name: Fishhouse Wall C
info.text: An empty lobster pot and a coil of rope. Whatever lived in the pot is in somebody's stew.

info.name: Fishhouse Wall D
info.text: Chalk tallies and a rusty anchor. One mark for every husband the sea kept; the widow stopped at thirteen.

info.name: Fishhouse Wall E
info.text: Salt crust, green slime and a notice with a red cross. The family moved out; the debt stayed.

info.name: Fishhouse Wall F
info.text: A harpoon stuck in the boards, still dripping. The argument about the catch is over.

info.name: Fishhouse Upper Wall
info.text: Weatherboards on the upper floor, silver where the wind has scoured them. Leaks only when it rains sideways.

info.name: Fishhouse Upper Wall A
info.text: A rope coil on a hook. In a fishing town everything is rope, and every rope has been a noose once.

info.name: Fishhouse Upper Wall B
info.text: A square of tar slapped over rotten boards. It holds until the next gale, then it holds the gale.

info.name: Fishhouse Upper Wall C
info.text: Rope and cork floats hung up to dry, out of reach of thieves and children.

info.name: Fishhouse Upper Wall D
info.text: Chalk strokes for the catches and red crosses for the boats that stayed out. The crosses are winning.

info.name: Fishhouse Upper Wall E
info.text: White streaks from the gulls. They aim, everybody says so.

info.name: Fishhouse Upper Wall F
info.text: A loose board nailed back on crooked. Good enough until the next storm.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Floor
info.text: Stamped clay with straw in it. Spill something and it becomes part of the floor.

info.name: Thatched Roof Slope, Right
info.text: Bundled straw over rafters. It keeps out most of the rain and none of the mice.

info.name: Thatched Roof Slope, Front
info.text: Bundled straw over rafters. It keeps out most of the rain and none of the mice.

info.name: Thatch Front A
info.text: Same straw, a hole the size of a fist. Something small is already moving in.

info.name: Thatch Front B
info.text: Same straw, a little more rot on the north side. Nobody has noticed. Nobody looks up.

info.name: Thatch Front C
info.text: Same straw, wearing its moss like a bad toupee.

info.name: Thatch Front D
info.text: The roof gave way here. The crow took the opportunity and has not left since.

info.name: Thatch Front E
info.text: Stripped to the laths. Someone ate the thatch. Someone else ate that someone.

info.name: Thatch Front F
info.text: Blood runs down the straw. The roofer fell, the roof held. Priorities.

info.name: Thatch Front Ridge
info.text: The ridge. Straw sticks up like a cheap wig; the wind has opinions about it.

info.name: Thatch Front Ridge A
info.text: The ridge. Straw sticks up like a cheap wig; the wind has opinions about it. Patched twice, trusted never.

info.name: Thatch Front Ridge B
info.text: The ridge. Straw sticks up like a cheap wig; the wind has opinions about it. Longer on one end, as if cut by a drunk.

info.name: Thatch Front Ridge C
info.text: The ridge. Straw sticks up like a cheap wig; the wind has opinions about it. Furry with moss.

info.name: Thatch Front Ridge+Gable L
info.text: The ridge falls apart at the left end. So does the roofer's excuse.

info.name: Thatch Front Ridge+Gable L A
info.text: The ridge falls apart at the left end. So does the roofer's excuse. Patched twice, trusted never.

info.name: Thatch Front Ridge+Gable L B
info.text: The ridge falls apart at the left end. So does the roofer's excuse. Longer on one end, as if cut by a drunk.

info.name: Thatch Front Ridge+Gable L C
info.text: The ridge falls apart at the left end. So does the roofer's excuse. Furry with moss.

info.name: Thatch Front Ridge+Gable R
info.text: Where ridge and gable meet, the straw gave up on straight lines.

info.name: Thatch Front Ridge+Gable R A
info.text: Where ridge and gable meet, the straw gave up on straight lines. Patched twice, trusted never.

info.name: Thatch Front Ridge+Gable R B
info.text: Where ridge and gable meet, the straw gave up on straight lines. Longer on one end, as if cut by a drunk.

info.name: Thatch Front Ridge+Gable R C
info.text: Where ridge and gable meet, the straw gave up on straight lines. Furry with moss.

info.name: Thatch Front Gable L
info.text: The left end of the thatch. It slumps over the boards like a drunk over a bar.

info.name: Thatch Front Gable L A
info.text: The left end of the thatch. It slumps over the boards like a drunk over a bar. Patched twice, trusted never.

info.name: Thatch Front Gable L B
info.text: The left end of the thatch. It slumps over the boards like a drunk over a bar. Longer on one end, as if cut by a drunk.

info.name: Thatch Front Gable L C
info.text: The left end of the thatch. It slumps over the boards like a drunk over a bar. Furry with moss.

info.name: Thatch Front Eave
info.text: The edge of the thatch, frayed and uneven. The roofer was paid by the day, not by the metre.

info.name: Thatch Front Eave A
info.text: A ragged eave. It sheds rain, mostly onto whoever stands under it.

info.name: Thatch Front Eave B
info.text: A crooked eave, one handspan too short. The roofer ran out of straw and patience.

info.name: Thatch Front Eave C
info.text: A mossy eave, sagging at the corner like a bad decision.

info.name: Thatch Front Eave+Gable L
info.text: Thatch on the left corner, in free fall for decades but never quite landed.

info.name: Thatch Front Eave+Gable L A
info.text: Thatch on the left corner, in free fall for decades but never quite landed. Patched twice, trusted never.

info.name: Thatch Front Eave+Gable L B
info.text: Thatch on the left corner, in free fall for decades but never quite landed. Longer on one end, as if cut by a drunk.

info.name: Thatch Front Eave+Gable L C
info.text: Thatch on the left corner, in free fall for decades but never quite landed. Furry with moss.

info.name: Thatch Front Eave+Gable R
info.text: Where eave and side meet, the thatch gives up completely. The corner is held up by habit and a bit of rope.

info.name: Thatch Front Eave+Gable R A
info.text: Where eave and side meet, the thatch gives up completely. The corner is held up by habit and a bit of rope. Patched twice, trusted never.

info.name: Thatch Front Eave+Gable R B
info.text: Where eave and side meet, the thatch gives up completely. The corner is held up by habit and a bit of rope. Longer on one end, as if cut by a drunk.

info.name: Thatch Front Eave+Gable R C
info.text: Where eave and side meet, the thatch gives up completely. The corner is held up by habit and a bit of rope. Furry with moss.

info.name: Thatch Front Gable R
info.text: The side of the thatch, hanging out over the gable boards. Nobody trimmed it. Nobody wanted to climb up.

info.name: Thatch Front Gable R A
info.text: The side of the thatch, hanging out over the gable boards. Nobody trimmed it. Nobody wanted to climb up.

info.name: Thatch Front Gable R B
info.text: The side of the thatch, hanging out over the gable boards. Nobody trimmed it. Nobody wanted to climb up.

info.name: Thatch Front Gable R C
info.text: The side of the thatch, hanging out over the gable boards. Nobody trimmed it. Nobody wanted to climb up.

info.text: Bundled straw over rafters. It keeps out most of the rain and none of the mice.

info.name: Thatched Roof Slope, Rear
info.text: Bundled straw over rafters. It keeps out most of the rain and none of the mice.

info.name: Thatch Rear A
info.text: Weathered straw bundles, tied and patched. The mice still refuse to pay rent.

info.name: Thatch Rear B
info.text: Weathered straw bundles, tied and patched. The mice still refuse to pay rent.

info.name: Thatch Rear C

info.text: Weathered straw bundles, tied and patched. The mice still refuse to pay rent.

info.name: Thatched Roof, Flat
info.text: A flat bed of thatch. Good for drying fish and hiding from tax men.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Window
info.text: A hole in the wall with a straw mat for a curtain. Keeps out the light, lets in the flies.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Window A
info.text: Boarded up from inside. Someone counted the days on the wall below. Then they stopped counting.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Window B
info.text: Dried fish on a string, and a rat nobody admits to. Dinner hangs where everyone can see it.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Window D
info.text: The shutter hangs by one hinge and the scratches below go the wrong way. Nobody asks who wanted out.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Gable
info.text: Boards nailed up under the end of the roof. They hold, mostly.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Gable A
info.text: Cracked clay between old timber rails. The repair is cheaper than admitting the roof is falling.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Gable Peak (down)
info.text: The other half of the timber gable. Nobody remembers which half was built first.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Gable Peak (up)
info.text: The pointed end of a timber gable. The birds nest here and pay no rent.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Gable B
info.text: Cracked clay between old timber rails. The repair is cheaper than admitting the roof is falling.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Gable C
info.text: Cracked clay between old timber rails. The repair is cheaper than admitting the roof is falling.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Tiers
info.text: Rows of plank benches. Splinters are free and so is the view of the killing.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Sign
info.text: A crooked board on a stick with a daub of paint. Nobody can read, so a picture of a sausage does the job.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Door
info.text: A plank door that sticks in summer and in winter. In spring it merely creaks.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Wall
info.text: Clay packed over a timber frame. Cracks come free of charge, draughts are included.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Wall A
info.text: A fresh daub of clay over last winter's hole. Still damp, still lumpy, still cheaper than a mason.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Wall B
info.text: A crack wide enough to post letters through. The straw inside is the only thing holding it together.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Wall D
info.text: A rat nailed up by its tail. Pest control, warning and decoration in one.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Upper Wall
info.text: An upper floor of clay on a crooked frame. The brace is the only straight thing in the house.

info.name: Mud-and-Timber Upper Wall A
info.text: A bird nests under the beam and pays its rent on the wall below.

info.name: Marble Floor
info.text: Marble slabs with a purple inlay. Slippery when wet, and it is always wet with something.

info.name: Marble-Slab Roof Slope, Right
info.text: Thin marble slabs with gilded seams. Nobody needs a marble roof, which is exactly why it is bought.

info.name: Marble Slab Right A
info.text: Pigeons have discovered marble. It is the only luxury they share with the owner.

info.name: Marble Slab Right D
info.text: A cracked slab. Marble is hard, but a falling tenant is harder.

info.name: Marble-Slab Roof Slope, Front

info.name: Marble Slab Rear D
info.text: A cracked slab. Marble is hard, but a falling tenant is harder.

info.name: Marble-Slab Roof, Flat
info.text: Flat marble slabs on top. Ideal for a terrace and for looking down on the street.

info.name: Marble Slab Flat A
info.text: Pigeons have discovered marble. It is the only luxury they share with the owner.

info.name: Marble Slab Flat D
info.text: A cracked slab. Marble is hard, but a falling tenant is harder.

info.name: Marble Window
info.text: A tall window with a bronze grille and a little gilded pediment. Bars, but tasteful ones.

info.name: Marble Gable
info.text: A marble gable, straight as a senator claims to be.

info.name: Marble Gable Peak (down)
info.text: The other gilded pediment edge. Symmetry costs extra and the owner paid.

info.name: Marble Gable Peak (up)
info.text: A gilded pediment edge. The gods look down from here, the owner looks down on everyone else.

info.name: Marble Tiers
info.text: White marble tiers for people who never sit on anything cheaper. The blood looks better from here.

info.name: Marble Sign
info.text: A bronze plaque on a marble pedestal. Whatever it advertises, you cannot afford it.

info.name: Marble Door
info.text: A bronze door with gilded studs. Heavy enough to keep out the mob and, on a good day, the creditors.

info.name: Marble Wall
info.text: Polished marble with a gilded band, paid for with somebody else's blood. Marble always is.

info.name: Marble Wall A
info.text: A crack filled with gilded putty. Patched like the reputation of the man who paid for it.

info.name: Marble Wall B
info.text: A donor's inscription, half chiselled away. He fell from favour; the wall only fell halfway.

info.name: Marble Wall D
info.text: Something red runs down from the gilded band. The owner insists it is wine. It is always wine.

info.name: Marble Upper Wall
info.text: An upper floor of polished marble. Up here the screams from the street arrive slightly muffled.

info.name: Palm-Leaf Roof Slope, Right
info.text: Layers of palm fronds, steep for the rain. It leaks only where you sleep.

info.name: Palm-Leaf Roof Slope, Front
info.text: Layers of palm fronds, steep for the rain. It leaks only where you sleep.

info.name: Stilt Bamboo Window
info.text: A slot in the bamboo, for air. The air here is mostly wet.

info.name: Stilt Bamboo Window A
info.text: Something drying in the window. It will never dry. Nothing here ever dries.

info.name: Stilt Bamboo Window B
info.text: A broken shutter, eaten by beetles. The beetles were eaten by the family.

info.name: Stilt Bamboo Window D
info.text: Hanging shutter, tally marks of a moneylender below. He reads them by torchlight from the boat.

info.name: Stilt Bamboo Gable
info.text: Gable poles, dark with rain and smoke. Something grows on them that has no name yet.

info.name: Stilt Bamboo Gable A

info.name: Stilt Bamboo Door
info.text: A door on stilts. The ladder is pulled up at night, along with any trust.

info.name: Stilt Bamboo Wall
info.text: Bamboo poles lashed with vine, on stilts above the mud. Below lives the damp; above lives the debt.

info.name: Stilt Bamboo Wall A
info.text: New poles beside old ones. The old ones are mostly mould now, holding hands with the new.

info.name: Stilt Bamboo Wall B
info.text: A split pole. Rain comes in sideways, gossip goes out the same way.

info.name: Stilt Bamboo Wall D
info.text: A small skull hung on a vine. Visitors are reminded to pay before they leave.

info.name: Stilt Bamboo Upper Wall
info.text: Upper bamboo wall under the palm eaves. Green with moss, proud of it.

info.name: Stilt Bamboo Upper Wall A
info.text: A nest under the beam. Whatever lives in it is smarter than the landlord.

info.name: Stilt Plank Window
info.text: A shutter propped open on a stick. Kick the stick and the conversation is over.

info.name: Stilt Plank Window A
info.text: A clay pot on the sill and a net on a line. Breakfast, laundry and evidence, all in one window.

info.name: Stilt Plank Window B
info.text: Shuttered tight against the mosquitoes, which have long since moved in.

info.name: Stilt Plank Window D
info.text: A red cross painted on the shutter. Fever inside. The neighbours row a little faster past this one.

info.name: Stilt Plank Door
info.text: A reed curtain and a ladder. Pull the ladder up at night and the house is a fortress, until the stilts rot.

info.name: Stilt Plank Wall
info.text: Salt-bleached planks on mangrove stilts. The tide comes in under the floor twice a day and takes whatever fell through the cracks.

info.name: Stilt Plank Wall A
info.text: A crab trap hangs under the floor. What it catches depends on who fell off the walkway last night.

info.name: Stilt Plank Wall B
info.text: A fishing net drying on the wall. It has caught fish, crabs and one tax collector.

info.name: Stilt Plank Wall D
info.text: Five strokes and a red smear. The moneylender keeps his books on the debtor's wall.

info.name: Stilt Plank Upper Wall
info.text: More salt-grey planks, higher up, where the smell of the mudflats arrives a moment later.

info.name: Stilt Plank Upper Wall A
info.text: Two crab traps on pegs. The crabs pay rent in claws.

info.name: Pantile Right
info.text: Curved terracotta tiles, cap over channel. One loose tile per storm, one dead passer-by per decade.

info.name: Pantile Right A
info.text: Sun-bleached tiles among the red. The roofer swears they are all from the same kiln.

info.name: Pantile Right B
info.text: Mismatched tiles from three demolished houses. Recycling, the landlord calls it.

info.name: Pantile Right C
info.text: Yellow lichen on old tiles. It has outlived four owners.

info.name: Pantile Right D
info.text: A broken tile and a hole beneath. The rain gets the bedroom, the rats get the rest.

info.name: Pantile Right E
info.text: Stones weighing down loose tiles. Cheaper than nails and good for throwing at tax men.

info.name: Pantile Right F
info.text: A dead crow on the roof. Nobody will climb up for it until it smells.

info.name: Whitewash Window
info.text: An upper window with green shutters. From up here you can see the arena and smell the tannery.

info.name: Whitewash Window A
info.text: Shutters closed tight, with a knothole at eye height. Someone up there is always watching.

info.name: Whitewash Window B
info.text: A pot of herbs on the sill. Dead since the last drought, still watered out of spite.

info.name: Whitewash Window C
info.text: Laundry on a line: a tunic, a loincloth, a rag of uncertain purpose. Nothing here is ever really clean.

info.name: Whitewash Window D
info.text: A birdcage on a nail. The bird stopped singing some time ago. Nobody noticed which day.

info.name: Whitewash Window E
info.text: A chamber pot on the sill, freshly emptied downwards. Look up before you walk below.

info.name: Whitewash Gable
info.text: A whitewashed gable. Pigeons rent it by the day.

info.name: Whitewash Gable A
info.text: A whitewashed gable with a dove hole. The doves are dinner, the droppings are décor.

info.name: Whitewash Gable Peak (down)
info.text: The falling verge, finished with a row of clay tiles. Rain runs straight into the neighbour's window.

info.name: Whitewash Gable Peak (up)
info.text: The rising verge, finished with a row of clay tiles. Wind gets in anyway.

info.name: Whitewash Gable B
info.text: A gable with a dove hole and the evidence running down from it.

info.name: Whitewash Door
info.text: An arched door of rough planks with iron studs. The studs are for the bailiff.

info.name: Whitewash Door A
info.text: The door stands ajar. Either they trust the street or there is nothing left to steal.

info.name: Whitewash Door B
info.text: A red curtain instead of a door. Cheaper than wood and just as useless against thieves.

info.name: Whitewash Wall
info.text: Whitewash over cheap brick on an ochre plinth. Every spring a fresh coat, every autumn fresh stains.

info.name: Whitewash Wall A
info.text: A window with blue shutters, so the neighbours can watch the executions without paying.

info.name: Whitewash Wall B
info.text: The plaster has given up here. The bricks underneath are no better.

info.name: Whitewash Wall C
info.text: A small window and an iron ring for tethering a donkey, a goat or a debtor.

info.name: Whitewash Wall D
info.text: A crack and a wanted poster, already crossed out. The reward went to whoever brought the head.

info.name: Whitewash Wall E
info.text: A bloody handprint by the door. Someone was looking for the medicus and found the wall.

info.name: Whitewash Wall F
info.text: A wall shrine to Grumulus, god of locked doors. Someone stole his head; he never saw it coming.

info.name: Whitewash Upper Wall
info.text: Plain whitewash on the upper floor. Up here the stains are older and the rent is lower.

info.name: Whitewash Upper Wall A
info.text: A small vent slit. It lets out the smoke and lets in the screams from the arena.

info.name: Whitewash Upper Wall B
info.text: Scaffold holes and a damp streak. The builders left in a hurry, the damp never left.

info.name: Whitewash Upper Wall C
info.text: A patch of fresh plaster over an old crack. Nobody asks what was behind it.

info.name: Grass-Grassed Roof Slope, Right
info.text: Dry savanna grass, bundled and tied. It burns beautifully, ask the last village.

info.name: Red Daub Window
info.text: A slot for light and gossip. The shutter is three sticks and a prayer.

info.name: Red Daub Window A
info.text: Strips of meat drying in the window. Whose meat is a question for the tax man.

info.name: Red Daub Window B
info.text: A broken shutter. Through it you can watch the cattle market, or be watched by it.

info.name: Red Daub Window D
info.text: The shutter hangs on one strap. Tally marks below count debts, not days.

info.name: Red Daub Gable
info.text: Gable boards bleached grey by a sun that has never heard of mercy.

info.name: Red Daub Gable A
info.text: Gable boards bleached grey by a sun that has never heard of mercy.

info.name: Red Daub Gable Peak (down)
info.text: Gable boards bleached grey by a sun that has never heard of mercy.

info.name: Red Daub Gable Peak (up)
info.text: Gable boards bleached grey by a sun that has never heard of mercy.

info.name: Red Daub Gable B
info.text: Gable boards bleached grey by a sun that has never heard of mercy.

info.name: Red Daub Gable C
info.text: Gable boards bleached grey by a sun that has never heard of mercy.

info.name: Red Daub Door
info.text: A plank door in a red wall. The hinges are leather, the lock is the neighbour's dog.

info.name: Red Daub Wall
info.text: Red earth, dung and spit, slapped on thick. The white zigzags are for luck; the luck is not included.

info.name: Red Daub Wall A
info.text: A patch of fresher daub. Somebody kicked the wall, and the wall kept the shoe.

info.name: Red Daub Wall B
info.text: Cracked in the dry season, cracked again in the wet. Ants rent the gap by the night.

info.name: Red Daub Wall D
info.text: A bleached cattle skull nailed by the door. The owner says it keeps lions away. No lions have complained.

info.name: Red Daub Upper Wall
info.text: Upper daub under the eaves, zigzag and all. Swallows dirty it faster than the painter can.

info.name: Red Daub Upper Wall A
info.text: A clay nest under the beam. Rent is paid on the wall below.

info.name: Adobe Roof
info.text: Packed mud on palm beams. In summer the family sleeps up here, in winter the scorpions do.

info.name: Adobe Roof A
info.text: Dates and peppers drying on a mat. Half for the family, half for the flies.

info.name: Adobe Roof B
info.text: Water jars on the roof, warmed by the sun to the temperature of soup.

info.name: Adobe Roof C
info.text: A fresh mud patch over a leak. It never rains, but one cannot be too careful.

info.name: Adobe Roof D
info.text: A roof hatch with a ladder. The only way out when the tax collector knocks downstairs.

info.name: Adobe Roof E
info.text: A little cairn with a rag on a stick. Burials in town cost extra, the roof is free.

info.name: Adobe Roof F
info.text: Bones bleaching beside a broken jar. Last week's dinner, or last week's guest.

info.name: Adobe Window
info.text: A small window behind a wooden lattice. Lets in air and lets the neighbours watch you sweat.

info.name: Adobe Window A
info.text: Shutters closed against the sun, the dust and the creditors.

info.name: Adobe Window B
info.text: A rug airing over the sill. It has seen better floors and worse stains.

info.name: Adobe Window C
info.text: Clay pots on the sill. One holds water, one holds poison, and nobody remembers which.

info.name: Adobe Window D
info.text: A bucket on a rope. Up come water and gossip, down go the scraps.

info.name: Adobe Window E
info.text: Broken lattice, torn cloth. Someone left through the window and did not stop to close it.

info.name: Adobe Window F
info.text: A horned skull above the window wards off the evil eye. The landlord still gets in.

info.name: Adobe Door
info.text: Planks and iron straps. Keeps the sand out and the tax collector guessing.

info.name: Adobe Door A
info.text: A patched curtain instead of a door. Burglars appreciate the honesty.

info.name: Adobe Door B
info.text: Left ajar to let the heat out. The heat refused to leave.

info.name: Adobe Door C
info.text: Strings of knotted rope against the flies. The flies have learned knots.

info.name: Adobe Door D
info.text: A red X on the door. Either the plague or the debt collector. Both come back.

info.name: Adobe Door E
info.text: Bones on a string rattle in the wind. Visitors take the hint.

info.name: Adobe Door F
info.text: A sandal nailed to the door. Its owner left in a hurry, and in pieces.

info.name: Adobe Wall
info.text: Mud, straw and patience, baked by a sun that hates everyone. Holds up the roof and, now and then, the neighbours.

info.name: Adobe Wall A
info.text: The plaster gave up before the owner did. The bricks underneath look honest enough.

info.name: Adobe Wall B
info.text: Red handprints for luck. The paint is ochre. Mostly.

info.name: Adobe Wall C
info.text: A water jar by the wall, sealed with a curse, because a lid costs extra.

info.name: Adobe Wall D
info.text: Rent, paid in instalments. The landlord keeps count on the wall, and on the tenant.

info.name: Adobe Wall E
info.text: An iron ring with a chain. For tying up camels, guests and debtors.

info.name: Adobe Wall F
info.text: A goat skull keeps evil spirits away. It did nothing for the goat.

info.name: Adobe Upper Wall
info.text: An upper storey on palm beams. Built tall, because the ground tax is charged per foot.

info.name: Adobe Upper Wall A
info.text: The plaster flaked off up here too. The bricks sweat less than the people.

info.name: Adobe Upper Wall B
info.text: An ochre zigzag frieze. Pretty, cheap and a little crooked, like the owner.

info.name: Adobe Upper Wall C
info.text: A wooden rain spout. It has been waiting nine years for rain.

info.name: Adobe Upper Wall D
info.text: A niche with a household god of clay. He takes every offering and never says thanks.

info.name: Adobe Upper Wall E
info.text: A chain and shackle on an iron ring. Some lodgers are not allowed downstairs.

info.name: Adobe Upper Wall F
info.text: Red tally marks: days since the last rain, or since the last escape attempt.

info.name: Sod Roof, Flat
info.text: A flat roof of living turf. The goats would graze it, if anyone here still owned a goat.

info.name: Sod Roof, Flat A
info.text: A smoke hole ringed with stones. Warmth goes out, snow comes in, the family stays in between.

info.name: Sod Roof, Flat B
info.text: Tent poles and hides laid out on the roof to dry. Moving house here means moving the roof.

info.name: Sod Roof, Flat D
info.text: A bleached horned skull on the roof. It keeps away evil spirits and, judging by the silence, the neighbours.

info.name: Sod House Window
info.text: A pane of stretched gut. You cannot see through it, which is a mercy.

info.name: Sod House Window A
info.text: The gut pane split and was sewn up again. The stitches are better than the ones on the owner.

info.name: Sod House Window B
info.text: Boarded up for the winter. Winter lasts eleven months.

info.name: Sod House Window D
info.text: A horned skull over the boarded window. Either a charm or a warning about the cooking.

info.name: Sod House Door
info.text: A stone lintel and a hide flap. You enter bent over, which suits the local tax collector fine.

info.name: Sod Wall
info.text: Stacked turf on a footing of field stones. Grass keeps growing in the wall, so the wall is technically a pasture.

info.name: Sod Wall A
info.text: Reindeer antlers over the wall. Proof of a good hunt, or of a hungry winter.

info.name: Sod Wall B
info.text: A hide stretched on a drying frame. It used to be a reindeer, now it is a coat with prospects.

info.name: Sod Wall D
info.text: A slaughter hook, a frozen red trail and some bones. Out here, nothing is wasted and nothing is cleaned.

info.name: Sod Upper Wall
info.text: More turf, piled higher. Rich families can afford to be buried alive a little further from the ground.

info.name: Sod Upper Wall A
info.text: Antlers on the upper floor as well. Somebody here is compensating.

info.name: Steppe Wattle Window
info.text: A hole with a shutter and ambitions. Lets in light, dust and the neighbours' arguments.

info.name: Steppe Wattle Window A
info.text: One shutter hangs by a single leather strap. The other went into the stove last February.

info.name: Steppe Wattle Window B
info.text: Stuffed with straw against the wind. Also against looking out, which helps.

info.name: Steppe Wattle Window D
info.text: A string of knucklebones in the window to scare off spirits. The spirits are reported to be unimpressed.

info.name: Steppe Gable
info.text: Sun-bleached planks under the eaves. Every one of them was a fence post before somebody needed it more.

info.name: Steppe Gable A
info.text: Patched with a darker board and one hopeful nail.

info.name: Steppe Gable Peak (down)
info.text: The falling end of the gable boards. Gravity does most of the carpentry.

info.name: Steppe Gable Peak (up)
info.text: The rising end of the gable boards, nailed down harder than the rest because the wind starts here.

info.name: Steppe Gable B
info.text: A bundle of steppe grass tucked under the gable to dry. Tea, medicine or mattress, depending on the week.

info.name: Steppe Gable C
info.text: A plank kicked out in some argument. The draught won.

info.name: Steppe Wattle Door
info.text: Planks, leather hinges and a horseshoe hung upside down so the luck drains out onto the doorstep, where it belongs.

info.name: Steppe Wattle Wall
info.text: Wattle, clay and a skirt of grass sods. The wind gets in anyway; so does the tax man.

info.name: Steppe Wattle Wall A
info.text: The daub fell off and nobody noticed for three summers. The wattle underneath is holding up the house and its opinions.

info.name: Steppe Wattle Wall B
info.text: Dung cakes drying on the wall: winter fuel, summer perfume. Out here even the smoke is second-hand.

info.name: Steppe Wattle Wall D
info.text: A horse skull nailed up for luck. It did not bring the horse much, either.

info.name: Steppe Wattle Upper Wall
info.text: Upper floor of wattle and daub, built by someone who had seen a second storey once, from a distance.

info.name: Steppe Wattle Upper Wall A
info.text: A hide stretched out to dry. Whose hide, the family declines to say.

info.name: Reed Stilt Window
info.text: A hole with a mat rolled above it. The mosquitoes use it as their main entrance.

info.name: Reed Stilt Window A
info.text: A gourd and a pot of brackish water on the sill. The water is for drinking. Good luck.

info.name: Reed Stilt Window B
info.text: The mat is down. Whoever lives here owes someone money, or a finger.

info.name: Reed Stilt Window D
info.text: A red rag over the shutter: swamp fever. The healer charges double for houses like this, payable in advance.

info.name: Reed Stilt Door
info.text: A rolled-up mat and one wobbly step. Visitors are announced by the splash.

info.name: Reed Stilt Wall
info.text: Reed mats lashed to rotten posts above the swamp. The damp climbs the wall faster than the rent.

info.name: Reed Stilt Wall A
info.text: A hole plugged with swamp mud and a cushion of moss. Wall repair, the local way.

info.name: Reed Stilt Wall B
info.text: Bundles of herbs drying under the eaves. Half are for fever, half cause it.

info.name: Reed Stilt Wall D
info.text: A jawbone and a string of finger bones against evil spirits. The last tax collector donated them.

info.name: Reed Stilt Upper Wall
info.text: Reed mats one floor up, slightly drier and considerably more expensive.

info.name: Reed Stilt Upper Wall A
info.text: Two eel traps hung out to dry. The eels did not volunteer either.

info.name: Mudbrick Roof
info.text: A flat roof of packed mud and straw. The family sleeps up here when the house gets too hot.

info.name: Mudbrick Roof A
info.text: Cracked by the sun. One more good rain and the bedroom gets a skylight.

info.name: Mudbrick Roof B
info.text: Fresh mud, laid last month. Already looks a hundred years old.

info.name: Mudbrick Roof C
info.text: Sand drifts in from the dunes every night. Sweeping it off is a job for the youngest debtor.

info.name: Mudbrick Roof D
info.text: Three water jars cooling on the roof. Counted every morning, twice.

info.name: Mudbrick Roof E
info.text: Dates drying on a palm mat. The flies got their share first.

info.name: Mudbrick Roof F
info.text: A hatch and the tops of a ladder. Pull the ladder up and the house becomes a fortress, for an hour.

info.name: Mudbrick Window
info.text: A small window behind a wooden lattice. Lets in a little air and a lot of gossip.

info.name: Mudbrick Window A
info.text: Shutters closed against the noon sun, the sandstorm and the neighbours.

info.name: Mudbrick Window B
info.text: A red rag hangs out to dry next to a pot of herbs. Both have seen better days.

info.name: Mudbrick Window C
info.text: A string of dried peppers. Hot enough to keep away flies, guests and the evil eye.

info.name: Mudbrick Window D
info.text: Bricked up and marked with a charcoal cross. Whatever was inside is not coming out.

info.name: Mudbrick Door
info.text: Palm planks under a palm-log lintel. Locked at night, which only slows the tax collector down.

info.name: Mudbrick Door A
info.text: A torn notice is nailed to the door. Nobody here can read it, which is probably for the best.

info.name: Mudbrick Door B
info.text: A goat-hair blanket instead of a door. Wood is for the rich and the dead.

info.name: Mudbrick Wall
info.text: Sun-baked mud, palm beams poking out at the top. Holds up the roof and, on a good day, itself.

info.name: Mudbrick Wall A
info.text: The plaster fell off years ago. Nobody replastered it, the bricks look honest enough.

info.name: Mudbrick Wall B
info.text: A crack, smeared shut with fresh mud. Repeat every spring until the house wins.

info.name: Mudbrick Wall C
info.text: The one rain of the year left its tracks under every beam. Locals still talk about it.

info.name: Mudbrick Wall D
info.text: An iron ring and a short chain for a camel, a goat or a debtor. The stain below is from one of them.

info.name: Mudbrick Wall E
info.text: A niche with a water jar. Stealing from it is a hanging offence, drinking from it a gamble.

info.name: Mudbrick Wall F
info.text: A water jar broke here. The wet patch is the most valuable thing in the street.

info.name: Mudbrick Upper Wall
info.text: The upper floor, mud on mud. Every storey is a bet against the next earthquake.

info.name: Mudbrick Upper Wall A
info.text: A wooden spout drains the roof. It has done so twice in living memory.

info.name: Mudbrick Upper Wall B
info.text: A coil of rope on a peg, ready for the well, the camel or the thief.

info.name: Brick Floor
info.text: Terracotta tiles, red and buff. They hide wine stains well and blood even better.

info.name: Tiled Roof Slope, Right
info.text: Red clay tiles in neat rows. One loose tile per storm, one dead passer-by per decade.

info.name: Tiled Right A
info.text: Moss has settled between the tiles. It pays no rent either.

info.name: Tiled Right D
info.text: A missing tile, covered with a plank and two nails. Good until the next storm, as everything is.

info.name: Tiled Roof Slope, Front
info.text: Red clay tiles in neat rows. One loose tile per storm, one dead passer-by per decade.

info.name: Tiled Front A
info.text: Moss has settled between the tiles. It pays no rent either.

info.name: Tiled Front D
info.text: A missing tile, covered with a plank and two nails. Good until the next storm, as everything is.

info.name: Tiled Roof Slope, Left
info.text: Red clay tiles in neat rows. One loose tile per storm, one dead passer-by per decade.

info.name: Tiled Left A
info.text: Moss has settled between the tiles. It pays no rent either.

info.name: Tiled Left D
info.text: A missing tile, covered with a plank and two nails. Good until the next storm, as everything is.

info.name: Tiled Roof Slope, Rear
info.text: Red clay tiles in neat rows. One loose tile per storm, one dead passer-by per decade.

info.name: Tiled Rear A
info.text: Moss has settled between the tiles. It pays no rent either.

info.name: Tiled Rear D
info.text: A missing tile, covered with a plank and two nails. Good until the next storm, as everything is.

info.name: Tiled Roof, Flat
info.text: A flat tiled roof. In summer the family sleeps up here, in winter the cat.

info.name: Tiled Flat A
info.text: Moss has settled between the tiles. It pays no rent either.

info.name: Tiled Flat D
info.text: A missing tile, covered with a plank and two nails. Good until the next storm, as everything is.

info.name: Brick Window
info.text: A window in a brick frame with green shutters. Ideal for emptying pots onto passers-by.

info.name: Brick Gable
info.text: A plastered gable wall. Pigeons rent it by the day.

info.name: Brick Gable Peak (down)
info.text: The falling half of a plastered gable. Rain runs down it and into the neighbour's window.

info.name: Brick Gable Peak (up)
info.text: The peak of a plastered gable. The highest point of the house and of the landlord's ambitions.

info.name: Brick Tiers
info.text: Tiers of stone seats. Bring a cushion, or rent one at a price that hurts more than the stone.

info.name: Brick Sign
info.text: A painted signboard with a red frame. It promises quality and is right about half the time.

info.name: Brick Door
info.text: A wooden door under a brick lintel. Knock twice; the third knock is always the debt collector.

info.name: Brick Wall
info.text: Plastered brick on a red plinth. Respectable enough to have debts.

info.name: Brick Wall A
info.text: The plaster has let go and the bricks show through. The landlord calls it rustic charm.

info.name: Brick Wall B
info.text: A list of names scratched in charcoal, each with a tally. Not a guest list. Nobody on it is invited anywhere.

info.name: Brick Wall D
info.text: A bloody handprint at shoulder height. Someone leaned here on the way out of a dispute.

info.name: Brick Upper Wall
info.text: An upper floor of plastered brick. The higher the floor, the cheaper the tenant and the longer the fall.

info.name: Thistle
info.text: A thistle with a purple crown. It stabs everyone who touches it and has never lost a fight.

info.name: Tall Grass
info.text: Grass up to the hip, dry and golden. Whatever hunts in it can see you long before you see it.

info.name: Reeds
info.text: Reeds at the edge of the water. Good for roofs, baskets and for losing a sandal.

info.name: Wildflowers
info.text: A handful of wildflowers. Pretty, harmless and trampled within the week.

info.name: Bare Earth
info.text: Honest dirt with a few pebbles. Everything you own will end up in it, and so will you.

info.name: Bedrock
info.text: Solid rock. Nothing grows here and nothing can be buried here, which makes it popular with neither farmers nor undertakers.

info.name: River
info.text: Brown in the cities, blue on the maps. Downstream, everyone drinks what upstream washed off.

info.name: River (current)
info.text: Swift, cold and in a hurry, like a debtor who just saw the gate open.

info.name: River (foam)
info.text: The froth is natural. Mostly. The tanners say so, and they should know.

info.name: River (drifting barrel)
info.text: A barrel heading downstream. Wine, nails or a tax collector; nobody fishes it out to check.

info.name: River (dead rat)
info.text: Belly up and still the best swimmer in the city.

info.name: Grass
info.text: Grass. It grows on anything, including last season's losers.

info.name: Dry Scrub
info.text: Thin grass, thyme and red dust. The ground here grows olives, goats and lawsuits.

info.name: Dry Scrub B
info.text: Grass baked straw-yellow. Thyme smells lovely, which is the only lovely thing for a mile.

info.name: Dry Scrub Red Earth
info.text: Bare red earth. Locals swear it was this colour before the last tax collector visited.

info.name: Dry Scrub Limestone
info.text: A flat limestone slab. Perfect for drying figs, sharpening knives or settling disputes.

info.name: Dry Scrub Old Bones
info.text: A skull and a rusty spearhead in the grass. The previous tenant left no forwarding address.

info.name: Dry Scrub Amphora
info.text: A broken amphora and a red stain. It is wine. Mostly.

info.name: Dry Scrub Cairn
info.text: A cairn with a stake and a red rag. Marks a boundary, a grave or a debt, depending on who asks.

info.name: Refuse Pit
info.text: The district's only public institution. It takes everything and never asks for papers.

info.name: Refuse Pit
info.text: A victory wreath lies on top. Somebody won something once and found out what it was worth.

info.name: Refuse Pit
info.text: The black puddle at the bottom has been there longer than the district. It may own it.

info.name: Refuse Pit
info.text: Dug by the residents, filled by the residents. The only project they ever finished.

info.name: Sand
info.text: Fine sand, excellent at soaking up whatever gets spilled on it. The arena uses the same kind, for the same reason.

info.name: Plank Walk
info.text: Two planks over the mud. The only paved road in the district, and somebody owns it.

info.name: Slum Mud
info.text: Mud, deep enough to keep a sandal and give back only the foot.

info.name: Greasy Puddle
info.text: A puddle with a rainbow on top. Nobody asks what made the rainbow.

info.name: Slum Puddles
info.text: Brown puddles that never dry. Children call them the sea. The sea would sue.

info.name: Open Gutter
info.text: An open gutter carries everything downhill to the neighbours. They return the favour.

info.name: Shards in Mud
info.text: Broken pots and pebbles. Every step is an archaeology lesson with blood.

info.name: Slum Ruts
info.text: Cart ruts full of brown water. The cart left years ago; the ruts stayed for the rent.

info.name: Trodden Straw
info.text: Straw thrown on the mud to make it walkable. It made it smell instead.

info.name: Waterhole
info.text: Fresh water, more or less. The men drink from it, the oxen stand in it, and nobody asks in which order.

info.name: Dirt Road
info.text: Packed earth with two cart ruts. Carts love it; whoever falls asleep on it will not love the carts.

info.name: Lifting Tripod
info.text: Three poles, a pulley and a winch. It lifts a block a hand high and keeps everybody's feet out from under it.

info.name: Wedged Block
info.text: Iron wedges in a row, waiting for the hammer. One hole is empty; the wedge is in somebody's boot.

info.name: Ashlar Stack
info.text: Squared blocks with the mason's mark. Each mark means one man's pay, so each mark is carved very large.

info.name: Ashlars on Sledge
info.text: Blocks on a timber sledge, ready to be dragged. One lost a corner on the way; it will be sold as rustic.

info.name: Rough Block
info.text: A rough lump straight off the face. A crowbar, a wedge of wood and a prayer are all it takes to move it.

info.name: Stone Chips
info.text: Chips and dust under the crane, and half a chisel. The other half went somewhere when it broke.

info.name: Quarry Face N
info.text: The quarry face, cut in steps. The wedges go in dry and come out wet; the stone splits along whatever line it likes.

info.name: Quarry Face E
info.text: The quarry face, cut in steps. The wedges go in dry and come out wet; the stone splits along whatever line it likes.

info.name: Quarry Face S
info.text: The quarry face, cut in steps. The wedges go in dry and come out wet; the stone splits along whatever line it likes.

info.name: Quarry Face W
info.text: The quarry face, cut in steps. The wedges go in dry and come out wet; the stone splits along whatever line it likes.

info.name: Quarry Face Pit N
info.text: Where a block came out there is now a neat hole. A temple somewhere has a new step; the quarry has a new ladder.

info.name: Quarry Face Pit E
info.text: Where a block came out there is now a neat hole. A temple somewhere has a new step; the quarry has a new ladder.

info.name: Quarry Face Pit S
info.text: Where a block came out there is now a neat hole. A temple somewhere has a new step; the quarry has a new ladder.

info.name: Quarry Face Pit W
info.text: Where a block came out there is now a neat hole. A temple somewhere has a new step; the quarry has a new ladder.

info.name: Quarry Face Slip N
info.text: A block tipped back and cracked, the rope snapped, and the red stripe on the face is not ochre. The block was a write-off too.

info.name: Quarry Face Slip E
info.text: A block tipped back and cracked, the rope snapped, and the red stripe on the face is not ochre. The block was a write-off too.

info.name: Quarry Face Slip S
info.text: A block tipped back and cracked, the rope snapped, and the red stripe on the face is not ochre. The block was a write-off too.

info.name: Quarry Face Slip W
info.text: A block tipped back and cracked, the rope snapped, and the red stripe on the face is not ochre. The block was a write-off too.

info.name: Banana Plant
info.text: A banana plant with a hand of yellow fruit. The monkeys took the ripe ones and left you the bill.

info.name: Flowering Bush
info.text: A bush with orange blossoms. The bees adore it; the men use it for something less poetic.

info.name: Bush
info.text: A plain green bush. Just big enough to hide a coward, as several have already discovered.

info.name: Hazel
info.text: A hazel shrub. Nuts in autumn, switches all year round.

info.name: Mastic Bush
info.text: A dark, glossy mastic bush with red berries. The resin sweetens breath; nothing sweetens the neighbours.

info.name: Broom Bush
info.text: Yellow broom in flower. Pretty, poisonous and used to sweep the arena floor afterwards.

info.name: Rosemary on Stones
info.text: Rosemary between stones. Good for lamb, funerals and hiding the smell of both.

info.name: Dead Bush with Helmet
info.text: A dead bush wearing a dented helmet. Its owner stopped here for shade and never needed it again.

info.name: Tamarisk
info.text: A pale tamarisk that drinks the ground dry. Thrives where everything else gives up, which makes it the patron shrub of debtors.

info.name: Tiled Roof
info.text: Red clay tiles over a plastered gable. Keeps the rain off the men and the men out of sight.

info.name: Toppled Column
info.text: Last year a hero, this year rubble. His name was chiselled off; his nose went the same way.

info.name: Toppled Column I
info.text: History is written by the winners and edited with a hammer. Mind the drums.

info.name: Column of Shame
info.text: Debtors and bad poets are chained here for the public to admire. Rotten fruit is sold at the next stall.

info.name: Column of Shame I
info.text: The iron collar is empty today. The crow is optimistic.

info.name: Column of Honour
info.text: A grateful city honours its benefactor, who paid for the column, the statue and the gratitude. The pigeons add their own tribute.

info.name: Column of Honour I
info.text: The benefactor raises his hand to bless the market. Or to point out who still owes him money.

info.name: Plank Shack N
info.text: Boards, a rag for a door and three stones to keep the roof from leaving. The rent is collected anyway.

info.name: Plank Shack E
info.text: Boards, a rag for a door and three stones to keep the roof from leaving. The rent is collected anyway.

info.name: Plank Shack S
info.text: Boards, a rag for a door and three stones to keep the roof from leaving. The rent is collected anyway.

info.name: Plank Shack W
info.text: Boards, a rag for a door and three stones to keep the roof from leaving. The rent is collected anyway.

info.name: Reed Hut N
info.text: Reed mats patched with mud. Keeps out the sun, the rain and most of the neighbours. Not the smell.

info.name: Reed Hut E
info.text: Reed mats patched with mud. Keeps out the sun, the rain and most of the neighbours. Not the smell.

info.name: Reed Hut S
info.text: Reed mats patched with mud. Keeps out the sun, the rain and most of the neighbours. Not the smell.

info.name: Reed Hut W
info.text: Reed mats patched with mud. Keeps out the sun, the rain and most of the neighbours. Not the smell.

info.name: Shard House N
info.text: Mud walls stuffed with broken amphorae. The wine is long gone; the jars still work hard.

info.name: Shard House E
info.text: Mud walls stuffed with broken amphorae. The wine is long gone; the jars still work hard.

info.name: Shard House S
info.text: Mud walls stuffed with broken amphorae. The wine is long gone; the jars still work hard.

info.name: Shard House W
info.text: Mud walls stuffed with broken amphorae. The wine is long gone; the jars still work hard.

info.name: Shack with Awning N
info.text: A stolen sail on two sticks makes a porch. Somebody sits here all day and calls it business.

info.name: Shack with Awning E
info.text: A stolen sail on two sticks makes a porch. Somebody sits here all day and calls it business.

info.name: Shack with Awning S
info.text: A stolen sail on two sticks makes a porch. Somebody sits here all day and calls it business.

info.name: Shack with Awning W
info.text: A stolen sail on two sticks makes a porch. Somebody sits here all day and calls it business.

info.name: Patchwork Shack N
info.text: Planks, reeds, a red cloak nobody will ask about. A barrel catches the rain and the drowned flies.

info.name: Patchwork Shack E
info.text: Planks, reeds, a red cloak nobody will ask about. A barrel catches the rain and the drowned flies.

info.name: Patchwork Shack S
info.text: Planks, reeds, a red cloak nobody will ask about. A barrel catches the rain and the drowned flies.

info.name: Patchwork Shack W
info.text: Planks, reeds, a red cloak nobody will ask about. A barrel catches the rain and the drowned flies.

info.name: Shack of Old Signs N
info.text: Built from a fishmonger's sign nailed on upside down. FRESH, it promises. It is not.

info.name: Shack of Old Signs E
info.text: Built from a fishmonger's sign nailed on upside down. FRESH, it promises. It is not.

info.name: Shack of Old Signs S
info.text: Built from a fishmonger's sign nailed on upside down. FRESH, it promises. It is not.

info.name: Shack of Old Signs W
info.text: Built from a fishmonger's sign nailed on upside down. FRESH, it promises. It is not.

info.name: Sagging Shack N
info.text: Held up by one beam, one rope and stubbornness. Do not lean on it. Do not sneeze near it.

info.name: Sagging Shack E
info.text: Held up by one beam, one rope and stubbornness. Do not lean on it. Do not sneeze near it.

info.name: Sagging Shack S
info.text: Held up by one beam, one rope and stubbornness. Do not lean on it. Do not sneeze near it.

info.name: Sagging Shack W
info.text: Held up by one beam, one rope and stubbornness. Do not lean on it. Do not sneeze near it.

info.name: Evicted Shack N
info.text: Door nailed shut, a red hand and a notice. The landlord got the hut back. The tenant got the street.

info.name: Evicted Shack E
info.text: Door nailed shut, a red hand and a notice. The landlord got the hut back. The tenant got the street.

info.name: Evicted Shack S
info.text: Door nailed shut, a red hand and a notice. The landlord got the hut back. The tenant got the street.

info.name: Evicted Shack W
info.text: Door nailed shut, a red hand and a notice. The landlord got the hut back. The tenant got the street.

info.name: Vomit
info.text: Last night's supper, returned unopened.

info.name: Vomit and Cup
info.text: Next to it the cup of the finest local wine. The stomach disagreed with the label.

info.name: Hash Press N
info.text: Hemp drying, a press squeezing, a wall full of chalk debts. Everybody here is relaxed except the creditor.

info.name: Hash Press E
info.text: Hemp drying, a press squeezing, a wall full of chalk debts. Everybody here is relaxed except the creditor.

info.name: Hash Press S
info.text: Hemp drying, a press squeezing, a wall full of chalk debts. Everybody here is relaxed except the creditor.

info.name: Hash Press W
info.text: Hemp drying, a press squeezing, a wall full of chalk debts. Everybody here is relaxed except the creditor.

info.name: Broken Handcart
info.text: One wheel left, the other sold. It still carries a load: the rags of its owner.

info.name: Bones
info.text: Gnawed clean. The dogs came second.

info.name: Ribcage
info.text: A goat once. Then dinner. Now a xylophone for children.

info.name: Soup Bone on a String
info.text: Dipped for a coin, pulled out for the next pot. Flavour guaranteed for another week.

info.name: Bone Heap
info.text: The leftovers of the cookshops. Soup has been made of them twice already.

info.name: Bone Heap with Dice
info.text: Bones for soup, bones for dice. The house always wins, and the house is a heap.

info.name: Cold Fire Pit
info.text: Stones, ashes and a kettle. The fire is out because the wood was eaten.

info.name: Soup Kettle
info.text: SOUP, says the board. A bone in the pot argues the point.

info.name: Droppings
info.text: Nobody owns a latrine here. Everybody owns a corner.

info.name: Droppings with Sign
info.text: A little sign says NOT. The rest of the sentence was stepped on.

info.name: Slab Shack N
info.text: Bark-edged offcuts the sawmill threw away, a sack for a door. The sawmill charges rent for the offcuts.

info.name: Slab Shack E
info.text: Bark-edged offcuts the sawmill threw away, a sack for a door. The sawmill charges rent for the offcuts.

info.name: Slab Shack S
info.text: Bark-edged offcuts the sawmill threw away, a sack for a door. The sawmill charges rent for the offcuts.

info.name: Slab Shack W
info.text: Bark-edged offcuts the sawmill threw away, a sack for a door. The sawmill charges rent for the offcuts.

info.name: Bark Hut N
info.text: Bark walls and a roof of turf. Grows mushrooms, moss and coughs in roughly equal measure.

info.name: Bark Hut E
info.text: Bark walls and a roof of turf. Grows mushrooms, moss and coughs in roughly equal measure.

info.name: Bark Hut S
info.text: Bark walls and a roof of turf. Grows mushrooms, moss and coughs in roughly equal measure.

info.name: Bark Hut W
info.text: Bark walls and a roof of turf. Grows mushrooms, moss and coughs in roughly equal measure.

info.name: Wattle Hut N
info.text: Sticks and mud, like a bird nest for people who could not afford a tree.

info.name: Wattle Hut E

info.text: Our Lady of Leftovers, built from what she was given. She answers no prayers but keeps all offerings.

info.name: Shrine with Offering Box
info.text: The offering box is locked. The priest has the key. The goddess does not.

info.name: Debt Post
info.text: Every chalk line is a debt. When the post is full, the debtor is sold to pay for the chalk.

info.text: Rags hung out to dry. In the slum they get wetter.

info.name: Line with a Toga
info.text: A senator's toga, purple stripe and all. It fell off a cart. Twice.

info.name: Water Barrels
info.text: Rain water, barrel water, puddle water. Drink fast and do not look.

info.name: Clean Water Mostly
info.text: The sign promises CLEAN, MOSTLY. The shoe in the barrel promises nothing.

info.name: Mandrake Bed
info.text: Dark star-shaped rosettes in black soil. Pull one up and you will hear about it. Briefly.

info.name: Mandrake Bed (dug up)
info.text: A fresh hole, a forked root and a torn rope on a stake. The rope did its job; the dog did not come back.

info.name: Bacchant Ground
info.text: Dark soil, purple stains and torn ribbons. Something was celebrated here, and nobody remembers what.

info.name: Bacchant Ground (puddle)
info.text: A puddle of wine and a dropped cup. It is wine. Probably.

info.name: Flower Beds
info.text: Flowers for garlands, temples and the graves of champions. Business is always blooming.

info.name: Flower Beds
info.text: Flowers for garlands, temples and the graves of champions. Business is always blooming.

info.name: Dye Garden
info.text: Madder for red, woad for blue. Senators wear the colours, the dyers wear the stains.

info.name: Dye Garden (spill)
info.text: Somebody tipped the woad pot. The soil will be blue until the next emperor.

info.text: Somebody tipped the woad pot. The soil will be blue until the next emperor.

info.name: Market Garden
info.text: Cabbages, onions, leeks and turnips in tidy beds. The tidiest thing a slave will ever own is a bed of leeks.

info.name: Market Garden B
info.text: Gourds sunbathing between leeks. They will end up hollowed out, like the gardener.

info.name: Market Garden (hoe)
info.text: A hoe dropped mid-row and a cabbage with holes. The caterpillars won this round.

info.name: Barley Field
info.text: Pale barley for bread, beer and gladiators. Gladiators are called barley men, and they hate it.

info.name: Barley Field B
info.text: Barley still green in patches. The brewer is already selling the beer.
